about: Reric (Gross Stromkendorf on the Wismar bay), the Obodrites' sea market, 793 to 811 and the empty shore after. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/reric.md, the spine and peoples/wendish.md. A draft for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not verified; local flags begin rr_. Woven into the region danes_norway on 7 Oct 2026 by the region's weaver: ties made to run both ways, people named in ties made real in their own ports or pointed at the right id, stories given beats and cards in the other ports, and the region's cards (encounters/danes_norway_793.json) named in the sites' 'do' lists.

ports.summary: Reric is the Obodrites' market on a low reedy shore at the bottom of the Baltic, and in 793 it is near its best years: straight lanes of sunken huts, more wells than any town of its size, and Wends, Danes and Saxons selling side by side. The land is the Obodrite prince's, but the due on every cargo goes over the water to the king of the Danes. A merchant comes for wax, honey, furs, amber, horses and captives, and brings iron, whetstones, querns, glass and anything Frankish; nothing is paid in coin, everything on the scale.
ports.seasons: There is no tide to speak of, no church and so no feast days: the year is counted by the ice in the bay, the first boats after it, the hay, the honey taken late in summer and the autumn killing of beasts. The market is a summer thing (?); in winter the Breitling freezes, the boats lie turned over on the shore and only the craftsmen stay at their pits.

history.text: The first settlement, about three hectares at the north end of the shore, with timber-lined wells set close together; the oldest timber was felled this year or the next.
history.source: Tree-ring dates of the wells, Gross Stromkendorf (Tummuscheit 2013, through de.wikipedia 'Reric')

history.text: In the 760s and early 770s the town moves south and is laid out afresh in a regular, chequered plan; the old northern ground becomes the grave field.
history.source: de.wikipedia and en.wikipedia 'Reric' (after Tummuscheit; Brather 2003); the year is the middle of the range

history.text: More wells are dug in the 780s than in any other ten years: the town is growing fast.
Witzan, prince of the Obodrites, marches with King Charles against the Wilzi.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 789 (from memory in the dossier (?)); de.wikipedia 'Drasco'

history.text: Witzan is killed by Saxons while crossing the Elbe at Hliuni to join the king. Thrasco follows him as prince.
Thrasco, with the king's envoy Eburis beside him, beats the Saxons from beyond the Elbe on the Sventana field.
The emperor empties the Saxon land beyond the Elbe and gives it to the Obodrites. The same summer Godfred, king of the Danes, comes to Sliesthorp with his fleet and all his horsemen.
By the emperor's order merchants going to the Slavs may go only as far as the named border posts on the Elbe road, and may carry no arms or mail for sale.
history.source: Capitulary of Thionville 805, c. 7 (MGH Capitularia I no. 44); chronicle_793.json 805-12-thionville-border-posts

history.text: New wells are dug in the town.

Godfred crosses with fleet and army, the Wilzi with him, and storms Obodrite strongholds at the cost of his nephew Reginold and many chief men. Thrasco flees; Duke Godelaib is taken by a trick and hanged; two thirds of the Obodrites pay tribute. Before he goes home the king destroys the emporium 'which in the Danes' tongue was called Reric, and which by the payment of dues brought great profit to his kingdom', carries off its merchants and sails to Sliesthorp.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 808 (the Latin read for the dossier; our rendering); chronicle_793.json 808-summer-godfred-abodrites, 808-summer-reric-destroyed

history.text: A well is dug: people are living here again. Godfred sends word to the emperor by merchants; the talks at Badenfliot come to nothing. Thrasco, with Saxon help, wastes the Wilzi's land, and is then killed 'by guile, in the emporium of Reric, by Godfred's men'.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 809 (our rendering); the well from de.wikipedia 'Reric'; the Moissac chronicle puts the death in 810 (chronicle_793.json 809-winter-thrasco-murdered)

history.text: Godfred is killed by one of his own following. Sclaomir rules the Obodrites.
The last dated timber of the town is felled. Nothing is built after it.
Louis the German kills Goztomuizli, king of the Obodrites, and shares the people among chiefs. The bay has no market that any text names.
Between this year and 945 the great rampart of the Mecklenburg is built, half a day inland (?); about 965 a traveller from Tortosa calls it Nakon's fort.
history.source: de.wikipedia 'Burg Mecklenburg' (tree-ring dates; Ibrahim ibn Yaqub)

history.text: The Wends rise against the Saxons and their bishops; the churches in their land burn.
The Christian prince Gottschalk is killed at Lenzen on the seventh day of June and the Obodrites go back to their own gods.

eras.text: The best years. Witzan is prince and marches with the Frankish king; the lanes are full from the first open water to the autumn killing, the smiths and bead-makers work with their doors open, and the Danish king's man takes his due at the shore without anyone raising a voice.

Witzan is dead at the Elbe and Thrasco rules. After the Sventana field in 798 his riders sell Saxon spoil and Saxon captives on the grass above the shore, and every Frank is asked, quietly, about blades.

The Obodrites have been given the Saxons' land beyond the Elbe and want ploughshares, seed and iron for it. Godfred has shown his fleet at Sliesthorp; boats from the Danish islands are counted as they come into the bay. From 805 the emperor's law shuts the land road to Frankish merchants, so more of them come by sea. New wells go down in 806.

Until the hay is in, an uneasy market. Then the king's ships fill the bay, the strongholds inland are stormed, Godelaib hangs and Thrasco is gone. The booths are pulled down, the merchants are put aboard with what they can carry, and the fleet sails for Sliesthorp. Craftsmen with nothing a king wants are left standing among the pits.

A third of a town. Those who hid or were not worth taking roof a few pits again and dig a well; a boat or two calls. Thrasco comes back in 809 and is killed here before the year is out. The last timber is cut in 811, and then the people go inland.

An empty shore. Reeds, low hummocks where the huts were, well shafts fallen in and dangerous to cattle, the grave field going under grass. Fishers from the villages inland draw their boats up here and do not stay the night.

The Obodrites' strength is at the great fort inland now, and their markets are elsewhere on the coast. Nobody on the shore can say what stood here or what it was called; the Danes still have the word, and no place to put it.

sites.name: The boat shore
sites.see: A long low shore of grey sand and reeds, boats drawn up stern to the water in a row, the island of Poel a dark line across the bay behind them. In front, men wade with wax cakes on their shoulders; gulls, the knock of a caulking mallet, the smell of tar, wet reed and smoked fish. The water hardly moves: there is no tide here.
sites.source: ARF 808 ('on the shore of the ocean'); de.wikipedia 'Wismarbucht', 'Blowatz' (Poel, the Breitling); no jetty has been reported, the harbour inlet is thought silted and partly lost to the sea (?)

sites.name: The king's awning
sites.see: A sail stretched over four posts at the top of the shore, a Dane on a chest beneath it with a folding scale hung from a spear shaft, two men with shields asleep against a boat. A heap of things taken in due lies behind him: a quern, three wax cakes, a bundle of marten. Wends pass it without looking at it.
sites.source: ARF 808: the dues of Reric profited Godfred's kingdom. The manner, the rate and the place of taking are not recorded: the awning and the scale are the game's (?). No toll house was found in the dig.

sites.name: The straight lanes
sites.see: Lanes laid out by line, so straight that a man at one end sees the bay at the other, with low reed roofs to either side hardly higher than his belt and goods set out on the roof edges. Honey in tubs, wax in grey cakes, furs on poles, a line of roped people sitting in the shade with a stout Dane walking up and down it. Three tongues at once, and the interpreter's fourth.
sites.source: The regular, chequered plan of the 760s and the sunken huts (en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia 'Reric'); the goods of the Slav coast in general, not shown by this dig (Herrmann 1985 through en.wikipedia 'Pomerania in the Early Middle Ages'); Slav boys bought by Anskar (Rimbert c. 15)

sites.name: The craft pits
sites.see: A row of pit huts with their doors propped open for the light. In one a man turns an amber bead on a bow drill; in the next a woman winds hot glass round an iron rod; outside, antler shavings lie like snow and a bronze-caster's clay moulds dry on a plank. Burnt horn, charcoal and the sweet resin smell of cut amber.
sites.source: Weaving, bronze-casting, glass beads, amber, antler and horn worked on the spot at a modest scale; huts that were dwelling and workshop in one (en.wikipedia 'Reric', after Tummuscheit)

sites.name: The iron pit
sites.see: A sunken hut blacker than the rest, its roof singed, a boy at the bellows and a smith who never looks up. Rivets, knives, fish hooks and a ploughshare half made lie on a stone; by the door stands a basket of long grey whetstones from the north, which he will not sell singly.
sites.source: Iron-smithing on the spot and hoards of whetstones of Norwegian schist (en.wikipedia 'Reric'); the ploughshare from the Obodrites' new land of 804 (ARF 804)

sites.name: The wells
sites.see: Square mouths of split oak let into the ground every few houses, each with a pole and a wooden bucket, the newest still yellow. Women wait their turn with yokes; a man waist-deep in a fresh shaft passes up buckets of grey clay. This is where the town talks: who has come in, what the Danes took at the shore, whose child is sick.
sites.source: Timber-lined wells, 127 samples and 70 dated to the year; the most in the 780s; 806, 809 and 811 the last (de.wikipedia 'Reric')

sites.name: The wrights' end
sites.see: The north end of the shore, where two hulls stand on blocks: one riveted in the Danish way, one pegged with wooden nails and caulked with moss. A steam trough smokes, oak chips lie ankle-deep, and a grey-bearded Dane and a young Wend argue across a strake with one word in three understood.
sites.source: Boat graves with rivets at the grave field (de.wikipedia 'Schiffsgrab'; the count is from memory (?)); Slav boats pegged with treenails and caulked with moss (peoples/wendish.md, Ralswiek). That boats were built here is likely and not shown (?)

sites.name: Dragomir's table
sites.see: A house above ground, the largest in its lane, with a table that is never cleared: bread, millet, smoked fish, a bowl of honey, mead in a wooden cup that goes round. No chest in the room has a lock. A woman with silver rings at her temples serves; another, sharper, sits at the end and turns every guest's words into the next guest's tongue.
sites.source: A table stands laid in every house, and a host is shamed who turns a stranger away (Herbord II.41; Helmold I.82: both witnesses of the 12th century, used here as custom (?)); no wine among them (Herbord II.1)

sites.name: The riders' field
sites.see: Trampled grass above the town where horses are picketed in lines and sold. When the prince comes down from the forts inland his men pitch here: round shields against a wagon, spears stacked, a fire, and one man with a Frankish sword sitting where everyone can see him. After 798 Saxon cloaks, brooches and people are sold here off the wagon tail.
sites.source: Thrasco is put at Reric once by the annals, at his death (ARF 809); that he came to his own market at other times is likely and not recorded (?). No hall is known here. Horses as the Wends' wealth: Herbord II.23 (later)

sites.name: The fenced oaks
sites.see: Three old oaks on a rise behind the town with a fence of split stakes round them and a gate nobody has shut. Inside the ground is swept. A strip of linen hangs from a branch, a honeycomb lies on a stone, a horse skull whitens in the grass. Nobody will tell a stranger the god's name, only that this land is his.
sites.source: The game's (?): no cult place was found at Gross Stromkendorf and no god is recorded for Reric. Modelled on the fenced oaks of the Wagrians, where anyone in danger of death was safe (Helmold I.83, 12th century). No Wendish god is named in any text before 1000

sites.name: The old ground
sites.see: The north end, where the first town stood: low mounds and flat graves in the grass, the dark ring of an old pyre, and here and there the long shape of a boat showing through the turf with a post at its stem. A horse lies buried beside one man, a dog beside another. Wend and Dane are a few paces apart, each in his own fashion.
sites.source: The grave field on the ground of the first settlement; boat graves listed for Gross Stromkendorf (de.wikipedia 'Reric', 'Schiffsgrab'). Burnt and unburnt burial side by side, horses and dogs, and the numbers are from memory of Gerds 2015 (?)

people.name: Dragomir
people.trait: An Obodrite trader in honey, wax, furs and people: careful with oaths, open-handed at table, and never forgets a service or a slight.
people.want: Frankish iron and a friend in the west who comes back when he says he will.
people.fear: The Danish king's ships in the bay; and a guest leaving his house hungry.
people.voice: Speaks through Liuba until he trusts you, then in rough Danish. Will not swear lightly, and says why.
people.looks: About thirty-five, wide-faced, brown hair cut round, a moustache, a long belted tunic and a fur-edged cap, a ring of twisted silver wire at his temple, a wax tally in his hand.
knows: what wax, honey and furs fetch here and what they fetch at Sliesthorp
which Danes in the lanes are the king's ears
the forts and the roads inland, as far as he will say
a cut silver coin with strange writing, and where it came from

ties.note: his prince, whose peace the market stands in
the king who takes the due, and in 808 takes him
they sell people in the same lane
his sister, and his tongue
pays him the king's due every boat, and counts what it comes to
a Svea who brought him the cut coin and weighs as carefully as he does
the same person
his wife Radmila, who keeps the table and tells him afterwards which guests to trust
after 808 the ale-wife at the Slie stood host for his household through the first winter; she has not paid for wax since
the man with the stick at the one gate, who paced out his plot and waits for the gift that is usual
thirty years of bargains with the old Danish wright and not one of them sworn
the well-digger built his house above ground, the only one in the lane
a young Danish wright from Skane mended a boat for him and was paid in wax and a good word along the coast

lines.greet: A Frisian. Sit, eat first. A man who talks prices on an empty belly gets the price he deserves.
lines.greet_again: You said you would come back with the open water, and here is the water and here are you. Liuba, the good mead.
rumour: The Dane at the shore weighs my wax for his king. I have asked what the king does for it. He says: he does not come.
They want me to swear to a bargain. Among us to swear is halfway to forswearing. Take my hand; it has never yet been wrong.
The Franks' law says you may sell me a cooking pot and not a knife to cut the meat. Your king is a careful friend.
lines.after_804: We are given the Saxons' fields. Fields want ploughshares. Bring me iron and I will not ask what shape it was first.
lines.after_808: Now I have four hazel rods at the head of the Slie, and a king. Here I had a lane and a table. Ask me which I would rather be asked about.
lines.saying: A guest sees in one evening what the host has stopped seeing in ten winters.
lines.farewell: Go with the south wind. If you meet Danes, you sold me nothing and I am a poor man.

people.source: The spine's cast.dragomir: invented, one of the merchants Godfred carried from Reric to Sliesthorp in 808 (ARF 808). At Sliesthorp from 808 (see that port); if the merchant hid him in 808 he is here again to 811 (chain reric_808). Name: Drago- + -mir. The Wends' unwillingness to swear: Helmold I.83; the hand: Thietmar VI.25 (both later)

people.name: Liuba
people.trait: Dragomir's sister, taken by Danes as a girl and bought back at fifteen with four tongues in her head: quick, unsentimental, and the one person in the town who hears everything twice.
people.want: To be paid for what she knows, not only for what she turns; and never again to be goods.
people.fear: A Danish sail she recognises. She does not say whose.
people.voice: Fast and exact in Danish, Saxon and passable Frisian; turns a man's words faithfully and then adds what he meant.
people.looks: About thirty, thin, dark brows, a linen headcloth with two bronze rings at each temple, a grey wool dress girdled high, a small knife and a bunch of tally sticks at her belt.
knows: who said what to whom in the lanes this week, in any tongue
enough Slavic to teach a patient man the market's words
what the Danes at the awning say when they think no Wend understands
the pens at Sliesthorp from the inside

ties.note: her brother, who paid her price and has never mentioned it
she knows his trade from the rope end and will not turn words for him
he knows she understands him; she knows he knows
she learned her Frisian at his pit, and he his Slavic from her
his wife is her cousin; the wells are where she listens
her brother's wife; they share a hearth and one opinion of Danes
turns the greetings that come over the water from the ale-wife in Skane, and adds what the skipper left out

lines.greet: You understand nothing here, I can see it. I am Liuba. A piece of silver the size of your thumbnail, and you will understand everything.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian who says 'honey' as if it were a sneeze. You are better than last year. Not good. Better.
rumour: The Dane at the awning told his man the king wants more than dues from this shore. He said it in Danish, in front of me, like a fool.
My brother feeds every stranger. One day he will feed the one who comes to count the houses.
A Saxon came through asking the road to the Danes. Baptised twice, he said, and it took neither time.
lines.teach: Listen. 'Med' is honey. 'Vosk' is wax. 'Ne' is no. With those three you can already be cheated properly.
lines.saying: The one who turns the words hears both lies.
lines.farewell: Go well. And when a Dane asks you what the Wends said, you had no interpreter that day.

people.source: Invented. Slav captives among the Danes: Rimbert c. 15. No source shows a Wendish woman merchant, so she is an interpreter in her brother's house. Temple rings are from later Slavic graves (?). The Slavic words are plain common Slavic, not attested for the Obodrites (?). Name: Liub-, a short name

people.name: Skardi
people.trait: The Danish king's man at the shore: patient, exact, alone among people who wish him elsewhere, and too proud to show that he minds.
people.want: The due in full and no trouble; a word of plain Danish from somebody who is not afraid of him.
people.fear: That the king will come himself one summer and ask why the takings are what they are.
people.voice: Says less than he means. Names a weight once. Calls the town 'the reeds'.
people.looks: Past forty, lean, a notch out of his upper lip, fair hair tied back, a blue cloak with a ring pin worn thin, a folding bronze scale in a leather bag round his neck.
knows: what every boat on the shore carries and what she paid
which king sits over the Danes this year and what he wants
the weights of the north and how silver is nicked and tested
when ships are being called up in the islands, a season before anyone here

ties.note: takes the due for him from 804; for the king before him until then (Sigfred (?))
the one man in the lanes who drinks with him
respects him, weighs his wax, and would not warn him
his mother's brother, who has lived here so long he counts as a reed himself
sends the takings across each autumn to the king's man at the Schlei (?)
another man of the same byname keeps the king's watch on Zealand; each is asked whether he is the other, and each says the other has the easier post (?)
knows she understands his Danish, and talks in front of her anyway; neither has decided who is using whom
the man at the Slie who takes the autumn's due and counts it without comment

lines.greet: A new boat. Lay it out on the sand, all of it. The king takes his part by weight, and I do the weighing.
lines.greet_again: You. Your wax was honest last time. Lay it out anyway; I am paid to look.
rumour: They ask why a Dane takes the due on a Wend's shore. I ask why the Wend pays it. Neither of us answers.
The king has been counting ships this winter. When a king counts ships, I would not buy a house near water.
I have sat under this sail eleven summers. The reeds have not learned my name. I find I know all of theirs.
lines.in_808: If I were a Frisian with a sound boat I would have business elsewhere before the hay is in. I have said nothing.
lines.saying: A scale has no friends. That is why it is believed.
lines.farewell: Fair wind. Tell them in the west the due here is taken once and not twice. It is more than they can say.

people.source: Invented: the toll-taker implied by the dues of ARF 808. Who was king of the Danes in 793 is Sigfred (?) (named 777 to 798); Godfred first in 804. Name: Skardi, 'notched', a Danish byname used as a name (names_placeholder.json)

people.name: Thrasco
people.trait: The emperor's friend among the heathen, and proud of it: a fighter who keeps his word to the Franks and his own gods at home.
people.want: Frankish swords for his men, which the law forbids from 805; and to hold the Saxons' land he was given.
people.fear: Godfred's ships in the bay, and the Wilzi at his back.
people.voice: Courteous to anyone from the west, through an interpreter; short with his own. Does not swear lightly.
people.looks: About forty, broad, dark hair cut round and a long moustache, a fur-lined cloak, a Frankish sword on a belt set with silver, guards with round shields and spears behind him.
knows: what the emperor has promised him and what has come of it
the Saxons beyond the Elbe, as an enemy knows them
how many ships the Danes can put in the bay, near enough
which of his own dukes he does not trust

ties.note: who drives him out in 808 and has him killed here in 809
takes his advice on what the market will bear
his sister's son and the captain of his riders (?)
the count at Dorestad is the nearest emperor's man a Frisian can carry word to
the dealer bought his Saxon captives in 798 and still owes for the last lot
the same person
the king of the Danes, who drives him out in 808 and whose men kill him here by guile in 809

lines.greet: You are from the emperor's country. Then you are a guest twice. Sit; my sister's son will see to your boat.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian who came back. Among us that counts for more than what he brought.
rumour: I fought the emperor's Saxons for him on the Sventana field. His envoy stood beside me. Ask the envoy how many came home.
The lord emperor gave me land beyond the Elbe. It is good land. It lies between the Danes and the Saxons, like a hand in a door.
Your law says no blades to the Slavs. I am the Slav who guards your emperor's border. Explain it to me slowly.
lines.in_809: I am back, and with Saxons at my side this time. Do not look so. A man goes home by the road that is open.
lines.saying: Count a man's horses, not his words.
lines.farewell: Go safely. If you see the emperor's count, tell him the Obodrite is still his friend, and still waiting.

people.source: Annales regni Francorum 795, 798, 804, 808, 809; chronicle_793.json. Real. The annals put him at Reric only at his death; his other visits, his birth year, the sister's son and the sword from the emperor are the game's (?). The saying on horses after Herbord II.23 (later)

people.name: Ratimir
people.trait: The captain of the prince's riders: young, loud, generous with other people's goods, and a better judge of a horse than of a bargain.
people.want: A sword like his uncle's. Failing that, a mail shirt. Failing that, the name of a man who sells either.
people.fear: Being left to hold a fort while others ride; and the Wilzi, whom he calls dogs a little too often.
people.voice: Loud camp Saxon picked up from prisoners; laughs at his own mistakes in it. Asks the price of everything he sees.
people.looks: In his twenties, long-armed, hair cropped, a short beard, a quilted coat with a Saxon brooch that is not his, a spear, a round shield with the paint knocked off one side.
knows: what was taken on the Sventana field and what is still unsold
horses: age, wind and price, at a glance
the forts inland and how many days each is from the shore
what the riders say about their prince when he is not there

ties.note: his mother's brother, whom he serves (?)
sold him Saxons on credit of a sort; neither agrees what is still owed
a Saxon aboard will know the brooch for what it is
they are from the same village inland
has heard there is a Frisian who puts blades in wine casks, and wants his name

lines.greet: Frisian! You have a Frankish knife. Is there a bigger one in the boat? No? Look again, I will wait.
lines.greet_again: My friend with the small knives. This time I have a horse for you that a king would steal.
rumour: On the Sventana field the Saxons ran into the river. We sold the cloaks dry. The owners were not consulted.
My uncle has the emperor's friendship. I have asked him what it weighs. He did not laugh.
The Danes came over the water with the Wilzi beside them. A man who hunts with dogs should count his fingers after.
lines.after_804: We have Saxon fields now and nothing to turn them with. A rider with a plough. My mother would be pleased.
lines.saying: A good horse and a bad road: you still arrive.
lines.farewell: Go. And if a cask of wine for me should clink when it is rolled, I will not be surprised.

people.source: Invented: one of Thrasco's men after the Sventana field (ARF 798) and the grant of 804. The Wilzi marched with Godfred in 808 (ARF 808). Name: Rati- + -mir (names_placeholder.json)

people.name: Stoimir
people.trait: The town's well-digger and carpenter: slow-spoken, stubborn, and sure that a place with good water cannot be ended by a king.
people.want: Sound oak, a sharp axe and somebody to pay for the next well. A whetstone from the north that he does not have to share.
people.fear: A shaft falling in on him; and, after 808, that he is digging for nobody.
people.voice: Few words, all of them about wood, water or weather. Reckons years by the wells: 'the one by the smith', 'the one after the Danes'.
people.looks: Stocky, clay to the thighs, a round felt cap, a short adze in his belt, forearms scarred white by rope, always a splinter of oak in his teeth.
knows: where the sweet water is and where the brackish
every house and who built it, since he did
which year anything happened, by which well was new
who stayed in 808 and where they hid

ties.note: his wife is her cousin
from the same village inland
learned to split oak true from the old Dane, and says so
built his house above ground, the only one in the lane
has heard the Danes at Ripa line their wells with old barrels and thinks it shameful (?)
mended a Wend boat with the old Dane's nephew one summer; neither would use the other's nails

lines.greet: Mind the hole. Water? That one by the lane is sweet. The one by the shore is for washing boats and Danes.
lines.greet_again: You are back. So is the water. Fill your casks at the new one; I want to hear what a stranger thinks of it.
rumour: Three new wells since the last hard winter. People do not dig where they do not mean to stay.
The old Dane says oak should be split, never sawn. He is right. I have not told him so.
When the first town was up at the north end my grandfather dug there. Now the dead have that ground. They do not drink much.
lines.after_808: They took the merchants and left the wells. A king can carry off a man. Let him try to carry off a hole.
lines.farewell: Go on. If you pass good oak going cheap, remember who lines the wells here.

people.source: Invented: the well-diggers and carpenters shown by 127 well timbers, with wells of 806, 809 and 811 after the fullest years of the 780s (de.wikipedia 'Reric'). Name: Stoi- + -mir (names_placeholder.json)

people.name: Toki
people.trait: An old Danish boat-builder who came for one summer thirty years ago, married here and stayed: belongs to neither people and is trusted by both.
people.want: To finish the boat on the blocks; and to be laid in his own boat at the old ground when the time comes, with somebody to see it done properly.
people.fear: That Skardi's king will make him choose a side before he dies.
people.voice: Understates everything. A boat that sank is 'wet'. Mixes Danish and Slavic without noticing.
people.looks: Near sixty, bent, white beard stained with tar, two fingers short on the left hand, a leather apron, a rivet hammer he never puts down, a small hammer of bone on a thong inside his shirt.
knows: every boat on the shore, who built her and what is wrong with her
the shoals of the bay and the way in past Poel in fog
how the Wends peg a strake and why he rivets his
the old kings of the Danes, and what he thinks of the new one

ties.note: his sister's son, sent here because the family already had a man in the reeds
taught him to split oak; lets him think he worked it out
they sailed in the same ship once, and neither says where
his brother's son Sote mends boats at the river mouth in Skane, and was taught here to respect a pegged hull
thirty years of bargains and not one of them sworn

lines.greet: That is a Frisian strake, and whoever fitted it was in a hurry. Pull her up. I will tell you what it costs to be ashamed of.
lines.greet_again: Still floating. I am a little surprised. Sit down; the trough is not hot yet.
rumour: The Wends peg their planks with wood and stuff the seams with moss. It holds. I have stopped telling them it should not.
My nephew weighs for the king. I build for anyone. One of us sleeps well.
I came here for a summer. That was before the lanes were straight. The mead is not even very good.
lines.ask: When I am done, see that they put me in the small boat, the one with the patched stem. Not the good one. Somebody can still use that.
lines.saying: Cattle die, and kinsmen die, and so one dies one's self. A boat only rots, which is slower.
lines.farewell: Keep the moss out of your seams and the water will do the same. Probably.

people.source: Invented: the Scandinavians who lived and died here, shown by boat graves with rivets at the grave field (de.wikipedia 'Schiffsgrab'; (?) for the count). His death in 806 is the game's. The saying turns Havamal 77 (Bellows 1923; texts_793.json). The bone hammer is a small amulet of the later kind (?). Name: Toki (names_placeholder.json)

people.name: Folcbern
people.trait: A Frisian bead-maker and amber-cutter from the terp country who followed the amber east and never went home: dry, exact, and starved of his own tongue.
people.want: Raw glass and broken cups from the Rhine to melt; news of the terps; somebody to say a Paternoster with once a year.
people.fear: Dying here unshriven, among people who would bury him kindly and wrongly.
people.voice: Dry Frisian, slower than at home, with Slavic words dropped in for things the terps do not have.
people.looks: Around forty, narrow, squinting from close work, burn scars on both hands, a short Frisian cloak he has patched for years, a small lead cross on a cord, an amber bead half-drilled between finger and thumb.
knows: what raw amber costs here and what a drilled string fetches at Dorestad
every Frisian and Saxon who has passed in ten years, and where they went
the craft pits: who makes what, who is good, who waters the bronze
who in the town was not taken in 808, since he was one

ties.note: taught her Frisian over the bead fire; she taught him to count in Slavic
a cousin on the mother's side at Dorestad, who thinks him dead (?)
the bead-makers at Ripa get Rhine glass first and send on what they do not want (?)
his raw amber comes down the coast on trust, a season behind, from a countryman at the Ests' lake, the Frisian Wigmar (?)
was baptised as a boy by a priest of Liudger's country, and remembers the words imperfectly

lines.greet: That is terp mud on your boots or I never saw any. Say something. Anything. I have not heard it spoken right since the last ice.
lines.greet_again: The countryman. Come down into the pit, mind the crucible. Did you bring glass, or only yourself?
rumour: They burn their dead here, or boat them, or bury them with a horse. I have told Liuba what to do with me. She wrote nothing down, naturally.
A king at home complains our cloaks are short. Here they think mine very long. A man should travel to be admired.
Amber is cheap where it washes up and dear where there is a bishop. I sit as near the first as I can bear.
lines.after_808: The Danes took the merchants. They looked into my pit, saw one man and a string of beads, and went on. I have never been so glad to be poor.
lines.saying: Drill slowly. The bead has all winter and so have you.
lines.farewell: God keep you, since nobody here will say it. And glass, next time. Broken is fine.

people.source: Invented. Frisians at Reric are likely from the goods and not shown by name (?); glass beads and amber were worked on the spot (en.wikipedia 'Reric'); the short Frisian cloak from Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34. Craftsmen left behind in 808 are the game's reading of the wells of 809 and 811. Name: Folc- + -bern

people.name: Radmila
people.trait: Dragomir's wife, who keeps the table that is never cleared and brews the mead for it: counts guests, not cups.
people.want: Honey enough for the brewing, salt, and a daughter married inside the lanes.
people.fear: The Danish sails her husband's sister dreams of.
people.voice: Speaks only her own tongue, and loudly, as if that would carry it over. Laughs when it does not.
people.looks: About thirty, broad-faced, a linen headcloth with three silver wire rings at each temple, an embroidered apron, a wooden mead ladle and a bunch of keys that fit nothing, since nothing here locks.
knows: who has eaten at the table this season, and who came back
what honey and salt fetch, and when the bees were taken
the mead: how long it has stood, and whose wedding it is for
what Liuba will not turn into Danish

ties.note: her husband; she feeds his guests and tells him afterwards which ones to trust
her husband's sister; they share a hearth and one opinion of Danes
an ale-wife over the water in Skane; they send greetings by every skipper and have done for ten years without meeting
after 808 the Danish ale-wife stood host for her household through the first winter

lines.greet: Sit. Eat. You are thin. All Frisians are thin. I have seen four.
lines.greet_again: You came back, so the mead was good. That was not the good mead. Today is.
rumour: The bees were taken late this year. The honey is dark. Dark honey makes the mead that men remember, and regret.
A table that is cleared is a table that expects nobody. Ours has not been cleared since my wedding.
An ale-wife over the water sends me greetings by every Danish skipper. I send mine back. One day one of us will find out what the other looks like.
lines.saying: Count the guests. The cups count themselves.

people.source: invented: Dragomir's wife (the spine: 'his wife wears several' temple rings), who serves at the table of the site reric.table, and the friend over the water of ahus.asbod's tie. The laid table: Herbord II.41; Helmold I.82 (12th-century witnesses, used as custom) (?); mead and no wine among them: Herbord II.1. Temple rings are from later Slavic graves (?). She goes to Sliesthorp with her husband in 808. The name is Radmila (names_placeholder.json)

stories.title: The king's due
stories.summary: For years a Dane weighs the due at the shore and a Wend feeds every stranger, and both are content. In the summer of 808 the king comes for the merchants themselves, and a Frisian who has eaten at Dragomir's table has a few weeks in which he knows more than his host.
stories.picture: A low reed-roofed town on a flat shore with a bay full of striped sails behind it; in front, a Wend in a fur-edged cap handing wax cakes down into a small Frisian boat while a woman looks over her shoulder at the water.

beats.text: Dragomir's booth: wax, honey and an order for iron tools, given with a hand and not an oath. Liuba turns the words and tells you afterwards what he did not say.
You come back with the iron, or without it. Either way there is a place at the table; but he remembers which.
Skardi weighs your cargo and says, to nobody, that a man with a sound boat might have business elsewhere before the hay is in.
Ships are being called up through the islands. Asulf knows where they are bound and what he expects to buy when they come home.
You can tell Dragomir alone, tell the prince's man, tell nobody and count the booths for the king, or simply load and go.
Sails in the bay, more than the shore has boats. The king's spokesman goes from lane to lane: every merchant is to load and follow.
The merchants of Reric are set down on the Schlei with what they carried. Dragomir asks one thing: who is still at home.
On Zealand the watchman at the king's landing counts long ships going out by the islands, shields inboard, and tells a Frisian he knows to be somewhere else by midsummer, and not east.
At the head of the Slie Dragomir has four hazel rods and a king. He asks every ship one thing, and has a tally cut for whoever will carry it.

endings.how: You went with the king's fleet and took a plot at Sliesthorp beside the Reric men.
endings.text: The house trades in the king's new harbour from its first summer. Dragomir is your neighbour and never quite forgives the ease of it.
endings.reward: A plot and a known name at Sliesthorp (chain reric_808, s11); the king's man friendly; Liuba cool.

endings.how: You warned Dragomir, carried his best goods west and brought word of his kin to him at Sliesthorp.
endings.text: He takes your hand in front of the other Reric men, which among them is a sworn thing. His house and yours buy and sell for each other from then on.
endings.reward: Sets gf_reric_friend; wax and furs at his price at Sliesthorp for life, and at half strength for your heir (chain reric_808, s12).

endings.how: You told the prince's man, and Dragomir's household went to the island in the Breitling before the sails came.
endings.text: The king takes the booths and not the people. In 809 a third of a town stands again, and the first roof up is his table.
endings.reward: Reric stays open to you, much reduced, to 811 (chain reric_808, s13); Dragomir, Liuba and Stoimir fast friends; the unlock reric.table_seat.

endings.how: You counted the booths for the king's man.
endings.text: The king's spokesman knows your name and pays in weighed silver. Liuba knows it too. No Wend at any market sits down with you again.
endings.reward: Silver and the king's favour at Sliesthorp (chain reric_808, s14); every Wendish person's feeling falls to wary.

stories.reward: A friend among the merchants of two towns, or a place in the king's new one: the chain reric_808 carries the cards.

stories.title: Twenty blades
stories.summary: Thrasco fights the emperor's wars with spears and Saxon spoil, and the emperor's law forbids any merchant to sell him a sword. He asks a Frisian for twenty blades and offers wax, honey, furs and his friendship: a crime, and perhaps a service.
stories.picture: A broad man with a long moustache seated on a wagon tail among picketed horses, one hand on the hilt of a single Frankish sword, the other open towards a Frisian skipper; behind them riders with spears and no swords at all.

beats.text: Ratimir asks first, loudly, as a joke. Then Thrasco asks, through Liuba, as a thing between the emperor's friends: twenty blades, no hilts needed, paid in whatever the boat will hold.
A blade may be sold to a count's man and to no stranger. A dealer who asks no questions wants silver by weight; twenty is more than he likes to sell at once.
The toll man's search. Thiadbod, who has never been caught, will say how it is done for a share, or will carry them himself for a larger one.
Skardi lays out every cargo on the sand for his king. He will find twenty blades. What he does about blades going to his king's enemy is a matter of what he thinks of you.
The casks are opened on the grass. Thrasco draws one blade, looks along it, and gives it to Ratimir without a word.

endings.how: You brought the blades past the toll and past Skardi.
endings.text: Twenty of Thrasco's riders carry Frankish steel when the Danes come in 808. It does not save the town. He says, in 809, that it saved him.
endings.reward: Sets sw_thrasco_armed and sw_ran_blades; a boatload of wax, honey and marten worth three times the blades; the unlock reric.princes_hand.

endings.how: You said no to the blades and brought ploughshares, axes and bar iron instead.
endings.text: Ratimir is disgusted. Thrasco is not: after 804 the new land beyond the Elbe is broken with your iron, and he says a friend who keeps his own king's law will keep faith with another's.
endings.reward: A fair price in wax and horses; Thrasco friendly; iron tools sell high here until 808; nothing for the count's men to find.

endings.how: You told Count Folcbert's steward at Dorestad what the emperor's ally had asked for.
endings.text: The steward writes nothing down and says the emperor's friends must be patient. At Reric the next year nobody mentions blades to you again, and Ratimir looks through you.
endings.reward: Standing with the count's men at Dorestad; Thrasco and Ratimir cool; the search at the toll goes easier for a year.

stories.reward: A prince's friendship and a cargo worth the risk, or a clean name and a quieter one.

stories.title: The cut coin
stories.summary: Dragomir wears half a silver coin on a thong: thin, broad, covered in writing no priest could read, brought by a Svea who would not say where he got it. He wants to know what the Franks would give for a bag of them.
stories.picture: A close view of two hands across a laid table: one holds up a half-moon of thin silver on a leather thong, covered in fine looping script, the other holds a small folding scale; a bowl of honey and a wooden cup between them.

beats.text: He takes it off and puts it in your hand. It is lighter than a penny looks and purer than a penny is. Liuba says the Svea called the makers 'the people of the south river', and that this told her nothing either.
Sigimar the moneyer turns it over many times. He will not say what it is. He will say what it weighs, what it would lose in his pot, and that he would like to see more.
Holmfast has a bagful, whole and cut, and counts them twice in front of you. They come up the eastern rivers for furs, wax and people. He will not say more for nothing.
You tell Dragomir what the Franks give. What you tell him is your own affair; Liuba watches your face while she turns it.
Skardi, asked and not argued with, teaches the weights of the north and the nick. He is so surprised to be asked that he does it properly. (Sets sv_scale.)
At the river mouth in Skane a caster keeps one piece of the same eastern silver uncut, and cuts a Frankish penny in two without a thought.

endings.how: You told him the moneyer's true rate.
endings.text: He nods, ties the thong again, and from then on sends his eastern silver west in your boat and no other, for a tenth of the difference.
endings.reward: Sets sv_first_dirham and sv_moneyer_trusts; a standing commission of silver to carry to Dorestad each summer to 808; Dragomir a fast friend.

endings.how: You named a lower rate and bought his next bagful yourself.
endings.text: It pays well, twice. The third summer a Svea at his table names the real price over the mead. Dragomir says nothing, and your place at the table is laid a little further down.
endings.reward: About a third over cost on two bags of silver; then Dragomir cool and Liuba's news closed to you.

endings.how: You admitted you could not judge it, and had Skardi teach you the weights and the nick.
endings.text: The Dane is so surprised to be asked that he does it properly. After that no northern buyer shorts you on the pan.
endings.reward: Sets sv_scale; Skardi friendly; test_silver without loss at any northern market.

stories.reward: A place on the silver road before most Franks know there is one.

stories.title: The spoil of the Sventana field
stories.summary: After the fight of 798 Thrasco's riders sell Saxon cloaks, brooches and people off a wagon above the shore. Six years later the same riders are farmers on the Saxons' own fields, with nothing to plough them with.
stories.picture: A wagon tail on trampled grass heaped with cloaks and brooches, a young Wendish rider holding up a woman's brooch to the light, a row of bound Saxons sitting behind the wheel, a stout Dane with a hazel switch pricing them by eye.

beats.text: Ratimir sells off the wagon: cloaks, knives, a silver brooch he wears himself. Asulf has first pick of the people. A Saxon aboard your boat, if there is one, will not come ashore.
One of the roped Saxons speaks to you in something near your own tongue. He is a smith's son from beyond the Elbe. He does not ask to be bought; he asks which way the Danes' country lies.
Saxons who would not be moved live among the Danes here. One of them is owed word of a brother last seen on a Wendish wagon.
The land beyond the Elbe is the Obodrites' now, by the emperor's gift. Ratimir wants ploughshares, seed corn and iron, and has horses and wax to give. He does not see why this is funny.
Seed and iron are bought up for the host every spring on the Saxon border. What is left can be had, at a price, by a man who does not say where it is going.

endings.how: You bought the smith's son and set him ashore among the Danes.
endings.text: He goes up the shore at Sliesthorp without looking back. Years later a smith there re-rivets your boat and will not take silver for it.
endings.reward: Sets sx_carried_fugitive; a friend among the Saxons at Sliesthorp; Brunger, if aboard, is yours for life; the count's men may hear of it.

endings.how: You brought ploughshares and seed corn for the new land.
endings.text: The first harvest beyond the Elbe is cut in 805 by men who were riders a year before. Ratimir gives you the horse he had been saving for a king.
endings.reward: A horse of the best kind and wax at source; Thrasco and Ratimir friendly; Brunger, if aboard, does not speak to you for a month.

endings.how: You bought the cloaks and looked at nobody.
endings.text: The cloaks sell well in the west. Somebody at Daventre knows the weave and asks where you had them, and you find you would rather not say.
endings.reward: A cheap cargo of Saxon cloth and brooches; no friend made and none lost.

stories.reward: The Saxon war seen from its far side, and a friend on one side of it or the other.

stories.title: Three wells
stories.summary: Stoimir reckons the years by his wells. He digs in 806 because the town is full, in 809 because it is not empty, and in 811 because he has always dug; and each time he asks the same returning stranger whether the water is good.
stories.picture: A man standing chest-deep in a square shaft lined with fresh yellow oak, passing up a bucket to a Frisian skipper; behind them only a handful of reed roofs, some fallen in, and a wide empty shore.

beats.text: He shows you which wells are sweet and which are for boats, and says a town is as old as its oldest well. He would like a whetstone from the north of his own.
A new shaft, the lining still yellow. He wants a stranger's opinion of the water and waits while you drink. The old Dane who taught him is dead this year and lies in a boat at the old ground.
Half the lanes are roofless. He is digging again, alone, for the thirty households left. He asks you to pay for the oak, since the men who used to are at Sliesthorp.
The last well. His wife's people are going inland to the forts. He has cut a mark in the bottom timber and will tell you what it is if you ask.
At the old ground a trench is cut the length of a small boat. The old Dane goes into it in the patched one, as he asked, with Danes and Wends standing a few paces apart.
At Ripa a well-wright lines his shafts with Rhine wine casks, hoops and all, and has heard that a Wend calls it shameful. He would like to taste the Wend's water.

endings.how: You paid for the oak in 809 and came back to drink from it.
endings.text: The mark on the last timber is your house's, cut beside his own. He goes inland with the rest. The well holds water long after there is anyone to draw it.
endings.reward: Sets rr_well_marked; Stoimir's friendship passes to your heir; the easter egg of the last timber; free water and news here to 811.

endings.how: In 811 you took Stoimir, his wife and his adze aboard and set them down where Dragomir is.
endings.text: At Sliesthorp the Reric men have a carpenter again, and the first thing he builds is a well. He says the water is not as good and digs another.
endings.reward: A fast friend at Sliesthorp who repairs your boat at cost; Dragomir and Liuba warm; sets rr_stoimir_west.

endings.how: You filled your casks and paid for nothing.
endings.text: He digs it anyway, with worse oak. The lining gives in the second winter. He does not blame you; he tells the story as one about wood.
endings.reward: Nothing lost. Nothing to come back for.

stories.reward: A man who measures time by your visits, and a mark at the bottom of a well.

works.name: A well lined at your cost
works.what: A square shaft dug to sweet water and lined with split oak, like the hundred others in the town, in a lane that has none. Stoimir digs it; the lane remembers who paid.
works.needs: Two visits, so that Stoimir knows you; silver by weight to the value named, or the same in iron tools.
works.gives: Water for the boat without waiting or paying (provision); the lane's news first (ask_news); the feeling of every Wend here a little warmer.
works.picture: Two men lowering a frame of pale split oak into a square hole while women with yokes wait at the edge.
works.source: Timber-lined wells, the most of any phase in the 780s and new ones in 806, 809 and 811 (de.wikipedia 'Reric'). That a stranger paid for one is the game's

works.name: A pit booth of your own
works.what: A sunken hut in the straight lanes, knee-deep, walled with wattle and roofed with reed, with a plank on the roof edge to show goods on. It stands in Dragomir's lane, under his word.
works.needs: Dragomir friendly or better, and the king's due paid at the awning every call.
works.gives: Goods can be left here between voyages (store) and sold while you are away at the market's price less a tenth for Liuba's trouble.
works.picture: A low reed roof in a row of others, hardly higher than a man's belt, wax cakes and a string of beads set out along its edge, a small door open on darkness.
works.source: Sunken-floored huts, dwelling and workshop in one, in a planned layout (en.wikipedia 'Reric'). It is lost in 808 with the rest

works.name: Withies on the bay shoals
works.what: Tall hazel poles with a wisp of reed at the top, driven into the sandbanks either side of the way in past Poel, so that a boat can find the shore in haze or failing light.
works.needs: Toki's knowledge of the shoals while he lives, or a pilot hired three times.
works.gives: No pilot needed into the bay (learn); a third less chance of touching in fog. Skardi approves, since it brings more boats to his scale.
works.picture: A small boat among calm grey shoals, a man standing in the bow driving a tall pole with a bundle of reed tied to its top.
works.source: The game's (?): the shoals of 793 are not known (the modern Lieps bank and Walfisch island are in de.wikipedia 'Wismarbucht'). Marking a channel with poles is the ordinary practice of shallow coasts and is not recorded here

works.name: A boat for Toki
works.what: The old wright is laid in his patched boat at the old ground with his hammer, his dog and a cask of the mead he said was not very good, and the turf is put back over the whole. It needs the boat bought from his heirs, a day's digging by many hands, and a feast after.
works.needs: Toki must have asked you (his line 'ask'), and you must be here in the year he dies.
works.gives: Skardi's lasting good will; every Dane in the Baltic markets who knew Toki has heard of it; a small deed of honour to the old gods' people.
works.picture: A small clinker boat sunk to its gunwales in a trench in the turf, an old man laid in it with a hammer on his chest, a mixed crowd of Danes and Wends standing round with cups.
works.source: Boat graves at the grave field of Gross Stromkendorf (de.wikipedia 'Schiffsgrab'); dogs and horses with the dead from memory of Gerds 2015 (?)

works.name: Roofs after the king
works.what: Reed, wattle and oak to roof a dozen pits again for the households that hid or were left, and a table set up in the largest.
works.needs: To have been known here before 808; the ending 'reric_holds' halves the cost, since Dragomir's people do the work.
works.gives: A lodging and a store here for the town's last three years; Stoimir, Liuba and Folcbern fast friends; the unlock reric.table_seat if you did not have it.
works.picture: Men thatching a pit hut with fresh reed among a dozen roofless hollows, a single table already standing in the open with bread on it.
works.source: The wells of 809 and 811 show the town mended after 808 by people who had three more years (de.wikipedia and en.wikipedia 'Reric')

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The Wends' own boat, pegged with wooden nails and caulked with moss, built by Stoimir's kin at the wrights' end. Cheap, dry and good in the shallows of this coast; Toki will tell you everything wrong with her.
ships.picture: A broad shallow clinker boat on blocks, pale wooden pegs in rows along her strakes, a man pressing moss into a seam with a wooden blade.
ships.source: peoples/wendish.md 6 (Ralswiek: four boats up to 14 by 3.4 m); ship_classes_793.json. That such boats were built at Reric is not shown (?)

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: Toki's work: a riveted Danish ship for sail and oars, of oak split and never sawn. He takes one order at a time and finishes when he finishes; after his death in 806 there is nobody here to build one.
ships.picture: A long lean hull on the shore with iron rivets in neat lines, an old man with a hammer sighting along her keel, a steam trough smoking beside him.
ships.source: Boats of 9 to 15 m from the rivets of the Reric boat graves (Design/content/ships.md; (?)); ship_classes_793.json

ships.note: A four-oar or six-oar boat off the shore, sold when its owner dies, drowns or goes in a bigger one. After 808 several lie ownerless and Skardi is not there to ask whose.
ships.picture: A small clinker boat lying turned over on grey sand among reeds, her oars pushed under her.
ships.source: Boat-owners buried in their boats (de.wikipedia 'Schiffsgrab'); ship_classes_793.json

ships.note: The fishers of the Breitling work from hollowed trunks. One will carry a man, his nets and a sack inland up the creeks where no clinker boat goes.
ships.picture: A dark hollowed log with a fisherman standing in it, poling through reeds at first light.
ships.source: The game's for this place (?): logboats are the common small craft of the Slav rivers and lakes (ship_classes_793.json)

sayings.text: The emporium which stood on the shore of the ocean and was called Reric in the Danes' tongue, and which by the payment of dues brought great profit to his kingdom.
sayings.source: Annales regni Francorum 808 (our rendering of the Latin). The Chronicle's own voice for the place: use it for the card that ends it

sayings.text: The Dane takes the due, the Wend sets the table, and the Frisian eats at one and complains of the other.
To swear is halfway to forswearing. Take my hand instead.
sayings.source: After Helmold I.83 (the Wends swear unwillingly, for fear of the gods) and Thietmar VI.25 (peace made with the right hand); both later witnesses, our rendering

sayings.text: He is strong, powerful and rich, for he has such or such a number of horses.
sayings.source: Herbord, Life of Otto II.23, tr. C. H. Robinson 1920 (said of the Pomeranians in the 1120s; used here as the Wends' way of counting a man)

sayings.text: If the dog is a strong one, he will bite hard.
sayings.source: Mistivoj of the Obodrites, in Helmold I.16 (our rendering; told of about 983, so a line for the later ages, not for 793)

sayings.text: Cattle die, and kinsmen die, and so one dies one's self; but a noble name will never die, if good renown one gets.
sayings.source: Havamal 77, tr. H. A. Bellows 1923 (texts_793.json): what the Danes say at a boat grave

sayings.text: A king can carry off a merchant. Let him try to carry off a well.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on ARF 808 and the wells of 809 and 811

sayings.text: They said it was not wise to kill a barefooted stranger, and let him go.
sayings.source: Ebo, Life of Otto II.1, tr. C. H. Robinson 1920 (Wolin, 1120s): the Wends' dry way with unwelcome guests, used as a joke told about themselves

easter_eggs.text: Stoimir cuts a notch in the bottom timber of every well. Ask him in the right years and he names them: the full year, the year after the Danes, the last. The wood remembers the years better than any man here does.
easter_eggs.source: The last wells are dated by their tree rings to 806, 809 and 811 (de.wikipedia 'Reric'): a nod to the method, in a person who cannot know it

easter_eggs.text: Nobody will tell you what the Wends call the town. Liuba says only that 'Reric' is the Danes' word, that it has to do with the reeds, and that the Danes name everything after the first thing they trip over.
easter_eggs.source: ARF 808: 'in the Danes' tongue'. The Wends' own name is not recorded; the meaning from reeds is a guess (de.wikipedia 'Reric')

easter_eggs.text: The smith keeps a basket of long grey whetstones under his bench and will sell them only by the dozen. They came from the north in one boat, and he is still waiting for the man to come back for his price.
easter_eggs.source: Hoards of whetstones of Norwegian schist in the town (en.wikipedia 'Reric')

easter_eggs.text: In 809 a Reric man at Sliesthorp will tell you, with some pride, that the king sent his word to the emperor in a merchant's mouth: 'He took us for our scales. Now he uses us for our tongues.'
easter_eggs.source: ARF 809: Godfred sent word to the emperor by merchants

easter_eggs.text: Toki, asked where the town will be in a hundred years, says the sea will have half of it and the grass the rest, and that men will look for it in three wrong places before they find it.
easter_eggs.source: The site was lost for a thousand years, sought at Oldenburg, Lubeck and the Mecklenburg, and found by the spade in the 1990s; part of the harbour is lost to the sea (de.wikipedia and en.wikipedia 'Reric')

easter_eggs.text: Ask how Thrasco died and every person here gives a different account, and all of them end with the same two words: by guile.
easter_eggs.source: ARF 809: 'per dolum'. How, by whom and on what day is not told, and the game does not say either

unlocks.how: Bring him the iron you promised, or tell him the true weight of the cut coin, or keep faith with him in 808.
unlocks.gives: Free lodging and store here (lodge, store); wax, honey and furs at his price; sets gf_reric_friend. Passes to your heir at half strength.

unlocks.how: Hire her as interpreter on three calls and pay what she asks without haggling.
unlocks.gives: tongue slavic = 0.5: no interpreter needed for buying and selling at any Wendish market; she begins to tell you what the Danes say at the awning.

unlocks.how: Bring him the blades, or the ploughshares and seed for the land beyond the Elbe.
unlocks.gives: The prince's peace on Obodrite shores to 808: his riders do not search or press you, and horses can be bought at the riders' field at source. Worth nothing, or less, with the Danes.

unlocks.how: Have him repair your boat twice, or set the withies on the shoals.
unlocks.gives: learn: the way in past Poel without a pilot, in any light.

unlocks.how: Bring him raw or broken glass from the Rhine and speak Frisian with him for an evening.
unlocks.gives: Amber beads and glass beads at the maker's price (buy_at_source), about a fifth under the lanes; after 808, word of who was left and who was taken.

unlocks.what: The northern weights, from the king's own man
unlocks.how: Ask Skardi to teach you rather than argue his weighing.
unlocks.gives: Sets sv_scale: test_silver and weigh_silver without loss at any market north of the Eider.
